title: Celebrating Earth Hour's 20th Anniversary

sections.heading: Body
sections.text:
Posted on March, 25 2026
The Eiffle Tower is among the world's iconic landmarks that went dark for Earth Hour. © Shérif Scouri / WWF France
After two decades of incredible global impact, WWF’s Earth Hour still offers you the opportunity to celebrate your love for nature and do something positive for the planet.
It all started on 31 March 2007.
WWF-Australia and the other Earth Hour founders had planned an innovative new way for people to register their concern about climate change. But would anyone join their symbolic switch-off of the lights over Sydney’s Harbour Bridge?
That night, 2.2 million people and over 2,000 businesses also turned off their lights, with Earth Hour making headlines around the world. Just one year later, the movement had spread globally, with 35 countries and major cities like Bangkok, Chicago, Copenhagen and Toronto joining in.
The rest, as they say, is history. A simple act of switching off led to the creation of what would eventually become the world’s largest grassroots environmental movement.
Around the world Earth Hour supporters go beyond the switch off and give an hour for Earth too. © Japhary Kiwanga / WWF-Tanzania
Positive action
WWF’s Earth Hour is now a much-loved tradition – an opportunity for people everywhere to come together to celebrate their love for the natural world and share their concerns about its future.
It also inspires individuals, communities, businesses and other organizations around the world to take action for the planet.
In the early years of Earth Hour, the movement focused on tackling the climate crisis. In 2009, for example, Earth Hour helped encourage over one million pledges for climate action.
More recently, the spotlight has shifted to the crisis of nature loss. In Argentina, Earth Hour support helped secure a 3.4 million hectare marine protected area in 2013.
In 2018, Earth Hour helped drive public momentum in French Polynesia, leading to the creation of a 5 million km² Managed Marine Area in its waters – a huge win for ocean conservation.
And since 2023, Earth Hour’s new campaign “The Biggest Hour of Earth” has encouraged individuals not only to switch off but also to Give an Hour for Earth − dedicating 60 minutes of their precious time to doing something positive for the planet.
Earth Hour 2025 saw a record-breaking three million hours pledged – an incredibly positive response we are so grateful for.
Earth Hour 2026
Saturday 28 March will be an incredible milestone – the 20th ever Earth Hour. And we hope you will feel inspired to join the celebrations with millions of others around the world.
We would love it if you could also commit to Give an Hour for Earth. Getting involved is really easy − whether you want to reconnect with nature, restore the environment, learn about the planet or inspire others to care for it.
